Title: Naming the SI Unit for Fracture Toughness (KIC) | iMechanica
# Naming the SI Unit for Fracture Toughness (KIC). In science and engineering, we have an excellent tradition: naming a physical unit using the name of a prominent personality from the concerned field. For example, in SI system, we measure force in newton, work in joule, power in watt... But the unit of fracture toughness, i.e. KIC, is too lengthy to pronounce: (mega) pascal-underoot-meter. Further, it has also been in use for something like half a century by now, perhaps more. So, how do you like the idea of giving a name to this unit? The physical quantity KIC is not necessarily the best measure of toughness... Please note, this is not a suggestion for a poll. ### 1 Griffith = 1 MPa.m^0.5. The units of KiC (i=I, II and III) look odd - MPa.m^0.5. I feel Griffith may be a good choice, because, the Fracture Mechanics starts with Griffith's theory and we encounter KIC there at the first time. In reply to 1 Griffith = 1 MPa.m^0.5 by ramdas chennamsetti. I do have an opinion on the matter, but would like to reserve it for the time being. I TOO AGREE WITH Mr. RAMDAS FOR RECOMMENDING THE NAME OF GRIFFITH AS A SI UNIT FOR FRACTURE TOUGHNESS. I have confusion between strain energy release rate, critical energy release rate and fracture toughness. The energy release rate is the reduction in elastic energy associated with a crack increasing per unit area of crack. This critical value is known as the fracture energy (also with dimensions of energy/length^2 or units of J/m^2). So, the energy release rate is the driving force for the advancement of the crack whereas the fracture energy is some sort of resistance to the growth of the crack. K is undetermined in the solution of the crack tip field and is a loading quantity that depends on the geometry of the boundary value problem. K has the dimensions of stress\*(length)^(1/2) or units of MPa\*(meters)^(1/2). As we can see, the stress intensity factor and the energy release rate are very similar conceptually. ### The griffith as the unit of fracture toughness...
